The three clocks don't form a ranking from worst to best — they answer three different questions (what happened, when the plant heard about it, when it was stored), and a pipeline that always prefers the 'most trustworthy' one regardless of signal is making a decision it never actually examined.

at.step: Reveal: three clocks, three different jobs

items.item: A clock that is never corrected mid-stream (the gateway's, the platform's) is monotone by construction, not by virtue of being more accurate — monotonicity and accuracy are independent properties, and this topic's device clock is simultaneously the most physically meaningful and the only one of the three that can go backwards.

at.step: Predict: can a backwards NTP step still land out of order?

items.item: An out-of-order timestamp is diagnostic information, not noise to be sorted away — the fact that it happened tells you a correction occurred between two readings, which a silent re-sort would destroy along with the anomaly.

at.step: Reveal: the step, measured

items.item: Storing an instant in UTC and rendering it in local time on demand is a decision to treat 'when' and 'how it's displayed' as two separable concerns — the moment a system stores local time without its zone, those two concerns become permanently fused, and no later process can safely separate them again.

at.step: Reveal: UTC stored, local rendered

items.item: A hard-coded shift table and a tz-database-generated one agree on every single ordinary day of the year, which is exactly what makes the hard-coded one dangerous: the two days it's wrong are rare enough that nobody notices until the wrong answer is already in a report.

at.step: Reveal: a calendar generated, not hard-coded

items.item: A ratio over 100 percent is never evidence the thing being measured exceeded its own ceiling — it's evidence that the number it was divided by doesn't match the thing's real scale, which is a denominator bug, not a numerator achievement.

at.step: Reveal: the same bug, in a different chapter

items.item: Recording which clock produced an event time, as its own column, converts an assumption a future reader would otherwise have to reconstruct (or guess wrong) into a fact they can simply read — the cost of that column is far smaller than the cost of someone re-deriving the choice from circumstantial evidence months later.

at.step: Reveal: choosing event time, and recording the choice

items.item: This chapter's earlier shift-boundary bug (topic 4, a downtime event crossing a shift change) and this topic's DST bug share the identical arithmetic shape — a fixed-length assumption meeting a boundary that doesn't respect it — which is why recognizing the shape matters more than memorizing either specific scenario.

at.step: Reveal: the same bug, in a different chapter

items.item: A system that reports a suspiciously clean, round, or unchanging number on exactly the days where real-world irregularity would be expected (both DST transition days reporting precisely 8 hours, all year) is reporting evidence of its own bug, not evidence of robustness.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: OPC UA's choice to expose both a source and a server timestamp, and let the client choose which to receive, is itself an acknowledgment that there is no single universally correct timestamp for a reading — the standard pushes exactly the decision this topic makes explicit (which clock is event time) down to the consumer, per request, rather than picking one for them.
